If you're a Steam Deck owner turned off from purchasing this game due to its "Unsupported" rating, don't be. I played through the opening Darth Vader level, and everything worked great! As for the game itself, it's a fun story where you get to experience what it would be like if Sith did not hold back. It can get repetitive at times, and the story is mostly skin-deep, but it's a fun time. I can't speak to the bugs and glitches that other users have mentioned playing it on a PC, but I would imagine that those would still be prevalent on Steam Deck, so that might be something to keep in mind.

Star Wars - The Force Unleashed has you play the role of Vader's secret apprentice, hunting rebels and Jedi down throughout the galaxy. While it sounds amazing, and in parts it is, this game has a number of issues resulting from being a console port: 30 FPS cap, clunky control scheme, and notoriously poor optimisation at launch (thankfully, this last point is not relevant on modern hardware).

In order to make this game playable, I suggest following the below guide (all credit to OP):
[url]http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=386753467[/url]
I played myself with the 60FPS file and did not experience any crashes during my playthrough, on Windows 10 Pro x64.

While there are still some very questionable design choices in this game (the Star Destroyer level comes to mind, as well as the Jedi mind trick section in the Jedi Temple DLC), for the most part, the game does a good job at making you feel like a powerful badass, destroying everything in your wake. The biggest pity about the story is the fact that it is no longer canon - although how much this matters to the average player is open to debate.

Recommended to Star Wars fans and those with some patience to get it working properly.

P.S. - The Star Destroyer level is significantly easier, in my experience, with the higher framerates - the TIEs seem to spawn in on a timer, and not on the progress you've made.

[h1]Star Wars | The Force Unleashed – Ultimate Sith Edition[/h1] ...is a spectacle-fighter platformer. Starkiller, Darth Vader's secret apprentice, is sent on a quest to create a diversion that will take Emperor Palpatine's attention away from Vader's own plans.

[h1]⚙ [u]Game Description & Mechanics[/u] ⚙[/h1]
You follow a specific story-driven list of levels, traveling to specific waypoints, jumping on platforms or following the path while encountering various waves of enemies. Attacks consist of your lightsaber, force grip, force push and force lighting attacks. You will often encounter mini-bosses such as a bull rancor, an AT-ST or a junk beast, which will first require you to deplete their life bar before finishing them off in a quicktime event. Each level usually ends with a boss fight such as a Jedi or a challenge of some sort.

Force points, which serves the role of experience points, are gained in different ways. You will get more force points from destroying enemies in a spectacular display of force. Completing secondary objectives will also award bonus force points. With each level, you gain force spheres for Force Talents (to increase your base attacks and defense), Force Powers (increasing their effectiveness which each rank) and Force Combos (to unlock increasingly powerful attack combos). Holocrons will also give you force points, force spheres, or lightsaber upgrades.

[h1]☺ [u]What I enjoyed[/u] ☺[/h1]
Assuming you take the time to upgrade your combos and learned them, you can do devastating attacks on entire groups of enemies. There are 27 combos to unlock, and many can chain up with each other. You may use a combo to launch an enemy in the air and shock them with force lightning, then a second combo to strike them multiple times mid-air, them another to slam them into the ground, and close with a force explosion that will send surrounding enemies flying to all corners of the area.

While the game's story was relegated to "Star Wars Legends", removing it from modern canon after the Disney acquisition of Lucas Art, it was a very interesting take on events taking place between Episodes 3 and 4, starting when Darth Vader was still hunting Jedi after Order 66, culminating with [spoiler]the founding of the Rebellion[/spoiler] with some recognizable characters making an appearance. Minor adjustments to Rogue One would have sufficed to keeping it in the lore, and it still holds pretty good today.

[h1]☹ [u]What bothered me[/u] ☹[/h1]
Each level consists of a narrow corridor or path with little to no branching path, making the level extremely constraint and the game terribly linear. Usually upon reaching a waypoint, something will prevent you from backtracking any further, so it certainly feels like a series of small levels. There is little enemy variety per level, often consisting of pallet swap with an additional skill or power. Mini-bosses repeat over and over, and always end with the same one or two mandatory quicktime event.

There isn't much variety in visuals, either, as most locations repeat: Kashyyyk, Raxxus Prime and Felucia are visited twice, and most imperial facilities look alike. They certainly don't hold a candle to games like [i][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/32370]Star Wars | Knights of the Old Republic[/url][/i] which was released years earlier. Time hasn't been too kind to it graphically, either, as the image quality shows its age. Furthermore, the game feels way too much like a port, with no mouse control in menus.

[h1][b]My Verdict[/b]: ★★★☆☆ - [i]"It's up to you."[/i][/h1]

Don't get me wrong: [i]Star Wars | The Force Unleashed[/i] is a good game, but it is by no means a great game, at least not by today's standards. You have a lot more "force" to work with than previous Star Wars action games had to offer, but if you don't have 15-year-old nostalgia, you'll want to lower your expectations to actually enjoy!

[i][b]This was just my opinion.[/b]

Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is an action adventure game releasing initially on PS2, PS3, Wii, Xbox360, iOS, Nintendo DS, PSP and who could forget, the N-Gage. The Ultimate Sith edition of the game finally released on PC and Mac OS in November 2009.   The plot in The Forced Unleashed is between the first two trilogies of Star Wars films, but acts as an original story.  You play the role of Darth Vadar’s apprentice, as you are tasked with hunting down Jedi – but you slowly become part of the Light side as things do not go as planned. 

The game play is very hack and slash style, with the good old classic lightsaber action and with a drop of force action too, the combat is very exciting and pack with all sorts of fancy attacks and duels. Part of your force powers includes the use of electric shocking your enemies too; this can be extremely pleasing to do on large groups of Stormtroopers. The combo system with the lightsabre is easy to get a grip of, and you can soon be showing off some crazy attacks, that look simply awesome.   The game does have quite a lot of QTE’s throughout, these normally occur at the end of a regular fight, allowing a more cinematic dramatic end to a fight, normally I am not a fan of QTEs, but these are done in a way which allow you to enjoy what is happening on the screen whilst also testing your speed and awareness of what is going on.

This game is old now, having released almost six years ago, the graphics are becoming to look a bit dated, but that’s not to say it is a bad looking game at all.  It is certainly not up to the standards we are used to now, but if you stick this on 1080p, you can still get some really nice looking scenes. The animation of all the characters are done brilliantly, and all of the levels look fleshed out with some really cool looking backdrops. 

Plot wise, this has got to be one of my favourite Star Wars games. I really enjoyed playing as the Dark side for once in this type of game, but you can’t stay as the Dark side, as events unfold, you soon start becoming part of the Jedi’s and working to over throw the Emperor.  It will really get you in the mood for watching the film series again. 

This isn’t a very difficult game; the only times I died were due to errors in the platforming side of the game and I ended up falling off the edge of the world. The difficulty can be ramped up, so playing on hard mode may be the way forward to get more of a challenge. The end boss fights pose a little bit of a challenge, but nothing that you can’t really overcome. I’m looking at you, Star Destroyer boss! 

Even though the game is very linear, the levels are all of a decent size, and have multiple paths to the end.  With plenty of hidden items for you to collect as you go, you’ll be jumping and fighting your way through plenty of enemies to find them.  I was a little disappointed to see that a couple of the levels were essentially the same map, just done in a different order so to speak, just seemed a little lazy on that part.
The game is also on the short side, having completed the game in just less than four hours on a normal difficulty. There is little reason to play it through for a second time unless you are trying the harder modes. 

I had a couple of technical problems whilst playing. I did go into the game expecting there to be some given the age of the game. The first issue I had was, even when selecting 1080p, the game still doesn’t play in a full screen, you get black bars down the side of your game, which are very annoying. Secondly, the game is capped at 30fps – I can only assume that is because it is a port of the PS3 game. Thirdly, the sound on some levels just cuts out for no apparent reason,  this has been reported as a common bug on the game, and a simple reload will fix it, so just an annoyance really.  I did also encounter a couple of random crashes which resulted in me losing a bit of progress – again I expected these due to the age of the title but would be nice if a patch could be released to fix the problems. 

To sum up, Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a pretty good action game. The game play is really good, and the plot alone all deserves your time and attention. The only thing that really lets it down is the length of the game. I would only say it is worth half of the £14, 99 price tag for that reason alone.  Due to the premium name of the game though it won’t go on sale very often so keep your eyes peeled.

[b]This is a long review, so if you want a brief summary of why I recommend [b]Forced Unleashed[/b] skip to [u]Results[/u] and read from there.[/b]

LucasArts offers a game that brings the force to modern-day systems; although, riddles with pitfalls in the design the Force Unleashed is still a fun and dynamic play-through. 

[b]Story:[/b]
You play a young Sith warrior who was taken under Darth Vaders’ wing to become his apprentice. You sole purpose in life is to become a powerful Sith warrior and join Vader to take down the Emperor and control the galaxy. Yet, not everything is how it seems and as you are sent from planet to planet to slay the remaining Jedi a whole new tale unfolds. 

[b]Campaign:[/b]
The campaign offers a decent length - depending on how you play it can take anywhere from five (5) to eight (8) hours. The story is divided up into approximately nine missions, which take you through a large variety of different environments. As you progress through the campaign you unlock new force powers, which change how you defeat your enemies. Each level has hidden Holocrons spread throughout it which offer you more experience, skill points, or customizable features. The enemies tend to repeat themselves fairly quickly and the combat dynamics become repetitive, but the bosses offer a nice twist which keeps you wanting more. Each boss fights differently, which causes you to constantly change up your strategy. 

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
The main issue with this game is the poor design. Firstly the camera controls are awful, there are more times where you are fighting the camera than fighting enemies. Trying to grab objects with the force can be rather cumbersome and I noticed that I never really grabbed anything because the time it took to get the object to move in the correct direction would cause me to take tremendous damage from surrounding enemies. Another major issue was being pinned by enemies, who would knock you over suddenly turning you into an elderly person who required a warm up before being able to stand up. 

[b]Hints:[/b][spoiler]
>Don’t play on the hardest difficulty (Sith Master) as the bosses scale poorly - the particularly Kazdan Paratus who was damn near impossible to defeat especially when fighting against the poor game mechanics. 
>Make sure to search the maps for the Holocrons they help you level up much quicker and afford you with more force powers.
>Remember to go in and look at your lightsaber, as you play through the campaign you unlock lightsaver powers which help boost your lightsaber. This can be really useful to change based on the mission you are playing. [/spoiler]

[b]Results:[/b]
All and all if you’re a Star Wars fan this is a game for you - if not them you probably find the listed cons to ruin the game. I personally like the Star Wars series and found this to be a good addition to the story even though some parts were cheesy. The game offers a decent sized campaign and a relatively fun experience. 

Pros:
+Customized level structure which allows you to choose how you want your character to grow.
+Lots of combos, which can make fighting incredibly dynamic.
+Control over many aspects of the environment, which you can wield in battle to your advantage.
+Awesome boss fights, which force you to change your play style.
+Beautiful level design with many different environments.
+Nice addition to the Star Wars saga, and great new story elements.
+Prologue was just awesome, walking around as Vader and destroying everything.

Cons:
-Not readily made for Keyboard and Mouse gameplay.
-Poor game design – difficult camera control, poor force power control, off targeting system.
-Limited to no description of objectives, can leave you standing around wondering what you’re supposed to do. I found myself shocking things with lighting, before realizing I had to grab them or slash it with a lightsaber. 
-Repetitive enemies, typically finding myself fighting the same thing over and over. This wouldn’t be bad, but some of them were more annoying than difficult to kill.
-Limited game customization, there was no ability to control graphics levels. Resolution was controlled before starting the game.

[h1] 9.7/10 [/h1]

Let's get this out of the way first: this game is an extravagantly unfinished piece of trash. 

It plays and functions like a very early and rough prototype, levels are spectacularly inconsistent in both length and difficulty, sounds and music many times fail to even load [!], it is locked at 30 fps [!!] (except for a glitch during combos that momentarily unlocks the framerate [!!!]), and textures and segments of levels fail to load at random times [!!!?!] (including during cutscenes when parts of the enviroment simply pop-in after the camera has already panned to it's location). It's undeniable proof of LucasArts's state of total disarray during the generation, and it's ridiculous this game was ever deemed release-worthy. 

However, I still recommend it....because I had fun with it and liked it. 

The story is fantastic; containing awesome moments, excellent plot twists, great original characters and deepening existing Star Wars characters. It contains a brand new original score that is wonderful and is up to the quality of John Williams' own work, and the graphics and rendition of the Star Wars universe is breathtaking and exciting once you get past the poor coding and glitches. The DLC for the game (included here) includes an alternative version of the Star Wars trilogy that is also really well done and pure fan service for any Star Wars fan. 

At the end of the game, I was left wanting for more....which is exactly what I want from any game. Go ahead and play it if you are a Star Wars fan, because you may have a blast.

Well, they weren't wrong about that. 
After playing it at my friend's house, I never expected it to have a lot of bugs, glitches, and crash issues.

I gave the game another shot when I saw it on sale, knowing I might experience the same thing. Thankfully, it's more playable than the last time I remembered it...of course with the help of a few tweaks. 

So far, here are my impressions after fiddling with the it:
- Xbox 360 controller option works like a charm.
- Keyboard and Mouse controls are a bit clunky, but not that bad at all if bound properly.
- You can only adjust the video resolution. Textures and other details of the game are still fixed.
- Visuals are good despite of its aging engine (played this on my HDTV).
- Loading screens on the options..everywhere.
- Camera controls are bad, but bearable.
- Force gripping/throwing enemies can be very entertaining.
- Boba Fett has a certain bug that makes him invulnerable unless you send him flying with force lightning.
- Seeing Ben Kenobi soaring and sliding across the screen after doing force combos is hilarious.
- Wampas are fragile creatures.
- Still full of bugs and glitches. Sometimes cool, most of the time funny.
- Applying the 60fps fix gave me a better experience while learning the lulz of the Force.
- I was able to fix my in-game crash issues by turning the cloth physics on and disabling the high details. Additional shadow and texture details were sacrificed in exchange of stability.

Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is an old game, and had quite a number of issues on the PC version. But as for me, it's not that bad if you apply the fixes and needed adjustments. It's still a great game and I've personally enjoyed every moment I had with it. 


Verdict (tl;dr)
If you already have Star Wars: The Force Unleashed (including the DLC's) on your PS3 or Xbox 360, feel free to skip this one. As for the fans who bought this game just like me, or who wish to get it while it's on sale, be sure to check the steam community forums. There you will find some guides and links for the fixes you'll need, including the missing sounds and the 60fps unlock. 

And if you're playing The Force Unleashed for the first time, you won't be disappointed. It has a well-polished storyline that any Star Wars fan would appreciate. Character customization is also a huge addition in this game. And last but not the least, the mix of lightsaber hack n' slash with the Force is fun as hell.

First off, I have a lot of nostalgia for this game, having played it many times when it first came out over 15 years ago. It's a good story with fun missions. 

With that being said, this game has not aged particularly well in it's current form. So be prepared for that, especially if you've played games like Jedi: Fallen Order & Jedi: Survivor. I hope one day this game will get a full remake with additional missions as the campaign feels a lot shorter than I remember.

The Force Unleashed games have received a fair bit of criticism over the years and I can understand some of those complaints. However, if you have ever thought to yourself, "Man, what kind of damage could you wreak on your enemies if you had the full weight of the Force to back you?" then you need to grab both games.

The Force Unleashed was the defining series of games during my early and mid-teens. I started by playing the version of the game for the Nintendo DS, which I still love the most. Outside of that, there are two other versions of the game: the sixth generation version for the PlayStation 2 and Nintendo Wii, as well as the seventh generation version for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and PC. In all of them, the story is mostly the same with some minor variations but honestly, I'd say this version of the game is definitely the weakest. The graphics are undoubtedly the best, but between technical issues, various gameplay quirks and the least amount of storytelling, this version just doesn't compete to the mind-boggling fun of the DS version or the sweeping epic that was the PS2/Wii version.

That being said, however, this game is still a phenomenal Star Wars experience. From start to finish, you can immerse yourself in this story and feel like you're in a standalone Star Wars film. You play as Starkiller, the orphaned son of a Jedi Knight, who ends up being recruited and trained by Vader as his secret apprentice. In the pre-Disney Legends timeline, Starkiller was one of the most powerful beings to ever exist, up there with Luke Skywalker, Anakin Skywalker and Darth Sidious. As a result of this, the majority of the gameplay involves you absolutely DESTROYING any enemies in your path. For the most part, the game's difficulty comes not from the mobs of enemies you face, but from quicktime events which can be extremely infuriating.

However, for the most part, the game is just a lot of fun. You throw your enemies around like rag dolls and it's extremely satisfying. Starkiller, voiced and based upon Sam Witwer (who would later go on to voice Darth Maul in future projects), is an awesome character that feels realistic, aside from his ridiculous levels of skill with the Force. Due to his upbringing under the tutelage of Darth Vader, he comes across as cold and emotionless but eventually begins to open up. His abilities make him a ruthless machine much like Vader, but a lot quicker and more agile due to his lack of a motion-inhibiting life support suit.

The story of the game is actually relatively enjoyable. It starts with Starkiller being assigned to kill remaining Jedi behind the Emperor's back but eventually expands to show us the formation of the Rebel Alliance and even includes an apperance by a particular character that is present in the much-lauded Thrawn Trilogy of books by Timothy Zahn. The main problem is how short the game is. Across the game's ~8 hour campaign, you experience awesome action moments, appearances by legendary Star Wars characters and a fun tale of revenge and hope. I prefer the Disney canon version of the story of the Rebel Alliance's beginnings (Star Wars: Rebels being my favorite piece of Star Wars content outside of the films), but this version is still extremely enjoyable and the developers at LucasArts (RIP) absolutely nailed that Star Wars feel, helping to immerse you in the story. True to LucasArts fashion, you have the choice to end the game with a good or a bad ending. The Ultimate Sith Edition tacks on some extra missions that take place after the bad ending, though I still have yet to actually play them as I tend to go for the good ending in games when I can.

The only real complaints I have about this version of the game are with the different level design and some technical issues, such as the game being framecapped at 30 FPS. I'm not one of those people that has to have 60 FPS in all games but when it comes to older titles like this -- especially ones that involve so much action and movements -- those sorts of things are a major issue for me.

To conclude, if you love Star Wars and want an epic action game where you're wreaking absolute havoc on your enemies, this is your game. Its sequel is, in many ways, even better with a more nuanced story, better graphics, more fine-tuned gameplay and much more entertaining scripted sequences.

Playing older video games on Steam is difficult to say the least. Technology changes, gaming PCs are able to process more and more with new titles, and developers move on from previous work. This has led to many games in the Steam library being incompatible with modern PCs (e.g. Max Payne 1 & 2, KOTOR, Bully: Scholarship Edition, Mafia (2002), etc).

This is the case with LucasArts’ poor PC port of their most ambitious Star Wars game: The Force Unleashed.

To get the game to run properly, I had to download a number of unofficial patches that included getting the game to run at 1080p w/ 60 fps. The unpatched, original release runs at a measly 30 fps, which is unacceptable, even for a game from a long time ago. Also, there were audio issues near the final levels of the game, which is irksome since the current patches have yet to solve 100% of the issue. Cutscenes are faint at times and exposition is hard to hear. Thankfully, the damage is lessened by fanmade fixes, NOT patches from Disney Interactive, who neglect other old Star Wars titles in terms of compatibility. This is a big problem throughout Steam and thankfully the community is vast so most of these games don’t die from obscurity.

With these patches, the game was definitely enjoyable. The bonkers force gameplay and good story elevate dated elements littered within the game. The passage of time has made this game feel antiquated. Cutscenes are shown in 720p and sharply contrast the HD level design and character models. Pop-up textures are constant, making the immersion lesser with janky moments. Some quicktime events and missions are tedious as well. However, The Force Unleashed is held together by some fun combat and absurd displays of Jedi magic. In the vein of Gears of War and Rock Band, this game is a time capsule of gamer past. A relic of old school genres. It isn’t dated, but quaint. Definitely nostalgic since I used to play this constantly on my Xbox 360, which honestly ran better than this incomplete port. However, it’s broken nature doesn’t subtract from some truly great gameplay moments and after completing the DLCs, I feel like I had fun trip down memory lane. 

Play this game on console. Trust me, it’ll save you a lot of time.

Did you like it when it came out 10 years ago?  Good, you'll like this as long as you follow this simple recommendation - use a controller.  It's a typical PC port and if you're familiar with them you'll immediately understand.  The game simply works better with the controller; menus, commands, tutorials - all are configured for the controller.  Just...grab a controller and you won't hate it.

Let's start with the good: This game is the original [i]Force Unleashed[/i] on steroids. The graphics are leaps and bounds ahead of the PS2/Xbox original, the game balancing is better, and the sound is much higher fidelity. Essentially everything else is unchanged, so if you've played the original game, you know what you're in for. The combat is absolutely phenomenal. The various Force powers are all incredibly satisfying to use, and both look and sound great. Chaining together different lightsaber+Force combos to deal massive damage is immensely fun, and thanks to a relatively sophisticated animation blending system for the period, they all flow together flawlessly into a brutal fury of death and destruction. They even animate your lightsaber striking/scoring the world around you [i]as you move around[/i] - not just when you attack shit. You can also dropkick Jawas at the press of a button (well, technically two), so that's another major selling point. 10/10 in my book. The port is also surprisingly functional, given the age of the game. I've experienced almost no major bugs or performance issues in my time playing it, on a Win10 x64 system. Obviously I can't speak for the relative performance of the Mac/Linux versions (do they even exist?), but the Windows version runs just peachy, and the framerate is buttery smooth (unlike TFUII, which is locked at 30 by default).

The meh: As with most games from the time period, the devs went absolutely balls-to-the-wall with the bloom and motion blur effects. To actually experience the visuals instead of looking at a horrid, washed-out mess, it's absolutely essential to turn bloom and blur off entirely (bloom is set via the in-game "Brightness" slider, while blur is set by the game launcher). Since the game is so old, it still runs at a positively buttery framerate on my modest 1060 rig, and the updated graphics in the Ultimate edition really make a difference in terms of overall quality, so you're not missing anything whatsoever by disabling them. While it's not gamebreaking, it is annoying to have to go out of your way to make the game look passable by modern standards.

The bad: The menus on the PC version are absolutely [b][i]atrocious.[/i][/b] The UI was very, [i]very[/i] obviously designed for consoles, and not only did they not change it [i]at all[/i] from the respective console versions, but the default key mapping is horrible too. It only reacts to the arrow keys and Enter for input - literally no WASD- or mouse-controlled menus whatsoever, which can be absolutely infuriating at times. On top of that, the in-game tutorials don't reflect any changes you make to the default binds, ie you bind something to spacebar but the in-game tutorials all still say Mouse1. While it still plays perfectly with a gamepad (arguably better than with a mouse and keyboard, for this kind of game), there's simply no excuse for how laughably bad the interface is.

[b]Final opinion:[/b]
No game since the Jedi Academy series has so effortlessly communicated the raw power of the Force. I can't communicate just how goddamn satisfying it is to fling stormtroopers around like twigs, it seriously never gets old. If you're just interested in several hours of solid, immensely satisfying eye-candy Star Wars action (this game lets you pick up enemies and throw them around in real time!!!), this game is well worth the asking price. However, it's still a platforming game from 2008. It can be janky as fuck at times, trying to jump with any kind of precision is harder than solid granite, the combat is punishingly difficult at times, and some of the dialogue is quite cringe-inducing. Worth it on sale, but not at full price. Pick it up only if you want a nostalgia trip from the original, otherwise skip it. It's a mediocre hack-and-slash platformer at its core - just one with a very, [i]very[/i] satisfying Star Wars paint job.

[h1]STAR WARS™ - The Force Unleashed™ Ultimate Sith Edition[/h1]
STAR WARS™ - The Force Unleashed™ Ultimate Sith Edition is the first part of Starkiller's journey; Vader's secret apprentice who will discover himself during the game. This version includes 3 extra missions as additional content along with the base game.
[h1]The Plot[/h1]
Before we start, this game is not canon in theory, but since I don't care about what Disney says, I personally consider this game canon, even though there are things about it that would definitely conflict with the main Star Wars narrative. It's basically God of War, only in space. We play as Starkiller, the son of a Jedi killed by Vader. Starkiller himself, despite obeying his master, feels a light side in himself, which leads to the main conflict. Not to mention the intricate intrigues of the Sith. The game itself tells the story of the origins and rise of the Rebel Alliance against the Empire, so we'll meet some characters from the original and prequel trilogy here. And even though the plot is pretty basic in the end, and a bit monotonous, and not very creative in some parts, it's okay, and I had fun. It is also worth mentioning that the game has 2 endings, one canonical that pushes us to the second game, and an alternative ending that gives us a different, darker ending, leading to additional missions, where we play as Darth Starkiller, who in an alternate reality leads the Imperial forces against rebellion as the Emperor's apprentice.
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
This is a very difficult thing to evaluate. On the one hand, we have a very good character development system here, which allows us to use a lot of power. The lightsaber combat itself is very good, you can really feel the power of the blows, the skirmishes are fast, lively and full of cool animations, and many options for approaching the fight. The ability to change the color of the lightsaber, and a really large number of cool costumes are also a good addition. The enemies are varied enough, but the lightsaber bosses are the most fun. The game is basically a fantasy of playing an invincible warrior who can tear entire armies to pieces by himself. Maps and mission conditions strive for variety, but towards the end of the game they feel a bit monotonous. What makes life very difficult for this game, however, is the fact that this game was built 100% for console. On PC, it's really hard to aim the force and the lightsaber, the controls themselves are tiring and it's hard to keep combat flowing. All this makes the game unintuitive and generally hard to play.
[h1]Technical Matters[/h1]
Apart from one crash and a few bugs related to the inability to peel off from some ledges, the game works stably enough. Graphically it's meh, the game has a weird, bland color palette which, along with the speed of movement and weird resolution of objects, made me feel like I was about to vomit most of the time. When it comes to visual effects, there is no craziness here either, but for the year of release, they are quite ok. The music is of course typical Star Wars movie music, so it is at a very high level. The cutscenes are very good, they are fun to watch despite the graphics, but what is most praiseworthy here is the great job of the actors who play all these characters. Their faces show a lot of emotion, but mainly their work in terms of voices is really high quality. Overall, the acting is on a really high level.
[h1]Summary[/h1]
A good game that is quite simple and achieves its goals, despite the many problems associated with the PC port. Personally, I don't think this game needed a sequel, especially since we're looking here at a very good conclusion to the rise of the Rebellion and the beginning of the Galactic Civil War.

The years have not been kind to the Force Unleashed. Oh yes - it is still the last word in ridiculously OP star wars kill-fests, but I find its janky controls and occasionally baffling mechanics have aged like flavoured milk. That said, the storyline, concepts, locations and characters remain top tier Star Wars. Mark Griskey's score is wonderfully original while paying homage to Williams, and its story of how the rebellion formed (which has been rewritten a million and one times now) is as good a version as you could ask for from an action game.  Give it a play if you're a fan of ludicrous rule-of-cool action sequences, quintessential Star Wars imagery, Sam Witwer (who provides voice and likeness for the main character) and all manner of sick expanded universe content.

It takes some mods to get working to today's standards but yeah, it's a good playthrough. It can get a bit repetitive after a while, and Juno's relationship with Starkiller feels really forced to me, but Sam Witner's performance is still good with what he's given. If you can take 10 minutes to get this game to run at 60FPS and add a physics fix file, then you'll likely enjoy this. I remember playing this on the PSP back in the day so this was a nice trip down memory lane for me.

Also the boss battles, some of them are not fun, and I will never understand the dev's wanting Euphoria as the physics engine when you end up just ragdolling during fights and you can't do anything but tank hits or die. 

The endings are pretty good, you can kill Palpatine and let him somehow return later, or go for Vader for a bad ending which is really grim. You get crushed with a ship, then metal armour gets grafted to your flesh and vocals it's really dark when you think about how painful that is. Sam Witner's shout if you choose that ending shows how good he is, and why he's so good as Darth Maul in the shows.

I don't know why this game gets negative reviews saying it's a bad port, then unironically quote things like the Wii version. It's a great game and a great port, there are multiple versions of this game because of what consoles could handle.

This one is, and I'm saying it in a positive way, a typical old-school game that has its own charm and aged well. I liked the lightsaber battles, and using the Force to crush through my enemies, it was great fun. Havok engine did its job well, and the ragdoll physics were hilarious as I picked up the little Jawas and threw them 50 meters away. :) As I mentioned before, the game's structure is pretty simple: follow the linear map, collect some extra holocrons, if you are up to it, you can also do one extra small "side mission" on almost every map, fight a lot, and that's it. You don't always need or want to collect and read 50 documents, gather 10 rabbit skins to an NPC, liberate all the outposts, and stuff like that. Also, it conveys the good Star Wars feeling that we love, so we know the people who made this love their work on it. Sam Witwer's talent is undeniable, and Matt Sloan as Darth Vader wasn't bad, either, but that's true about the whole voice cast.

Some proactive critics: the story altogether was descent, even if sometimes was cliché, but I think some major parts of Starkiller's arc was underwritten, and in some parts they reused moments from the Original trilogy and repeated them here, which I believe didn't work at all, we've all seen this before, and if you repeat a previously used element at a big moment just to bow before the past, or to do some nostalgia or something like that, well, usually it's not working. Another big problem: why the heck wasn't a huge plot twist I could read in one of the NPCs' backstories at the beginning of the game? There was another one, but at least that was revealed soon after. It reminded me of Jedi: Survivor when I checked the database of the enemy types and saw something that I shouldn't have.
And almost the same about the music, although there are some original tracks, but mostly we just hear the same old melodies from the original score. Have no fear about it, John Williams is a beast, it's always a bliss to listen to his masterpieces, but those titles were created for different characters and moments. And I still believe we don't need to always hear the Force theme whenever it would seem appropriate. Again, the Jedi games did it right; they created new themes for everyone and barely touched the previous music - or if they did, it might have been a newish version of it.

Alas, the PC version would need a major graphical update, perhaps a remaster, because it's buggy, glitchy, the objects were stuttering, etc., and the game crashed a few times, so I experienced all the "fun" things here I could.

There are a few technical problems depending on how you look at it may not seem like the end of the world, once you get to the second junk yard level the games music and some of the sound effects just stops working. the game is locked on a rocky 30 frames per second and even if you do want to fix these things I don't recommend it. doing it will just make the game shit its pants. Overall I would rate this game a 7/10 because of it's fun gameplay but lack of replay value.

Ever dreamed of becoming a wielder of the Force? Well here is practically a simulation as a master of the Dark Side of the Force. You play as Darth Vader's apprentice, Galen Marek as you trawl through the galaxy as you blast your enemies away with varieties of different powers and complex light-saber combos. The levels are lengthy and well designed with unique atmospheres and terrains that guarantee exciting game-play. No matter what challenge you face you are almost always able to get take care of the depending on how you level up your powers, combos, and talents. While not a perfect game (levels can sometimes get stale and repetitious, enemies can be rather uninspired), Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a fun pick-up-and-play type of game.

From a technical aspect, this game really did wonders and blew me away at the time of its release. The devs implemented a simulation/motion engine and 2 physics engines (Euphoria, Havok and DMM respectively) which goverened animations and movement, object collision, and material deformation/destruction. They managed to make all three work in tandem and interact with one another, which made for a semi-rEaLiSTic gameplay experience. On top of that, you play as an overpowered Force wielder with unbridled abilities and are thrown into this playground to wreck havok (pun)

Your Force powers are the best part of the whole game. You have most of the Force abilities you'd come to expect like Lightning, Lightsaber throws and your Force grip/push - no choking, so you'll have to look elsewhere if you're into that. Your Force Lightning will definitely be your go-to ability in most fights and I'll get into why later. You'll be able to upgrade these abilities so you'll become somewhat stronger as you progress. With these abilities you can lift your enemies in the air and watch them flail around and launch them hundreds of meters away, shove objects into them and yadda yadda. Enemies, when lifted with The Force, will latch on to nearby objects or enemies and will either: 
(a) bring the object/enemy with them or (b) resist being pulled/lifted any further if the object they're grabbing onto is anchored to the ground.
They can also dive out of the way of incoming objects. This behaviour is thanks to the Euphoria engine - which was also used in GTA IV and almost every Rockstar game after it and automatically makes any game more fun. So what's wrong with this game? 

A [i] lot [/i]

[h1] The Bad [/h1]
Where do I begin... I guess we'll start with the performance. 
-Capped at 30 fps which isn't a big deal to me but might be to you. There should be a guide somewhere on how to unlock the framerate.
-Crashes. I've only encountered 2-3 in my entire playthrough. They only happened when I was 1-2 
hours into each session. 
-Weird mouse + keyboard controls - you might want to use a controller.
-Input glitches? Sometimes when I press and hold down the Lightning button, which is Y or Triangle in my case, the game would only register it as a tap. So instead on continually electricuting my enemies until I let go of the button, Starkiller would just electricute them for half a second and stop, despite me holding down the button. This happened on multiple occasions and kinda annoyed me.

Now into the nitty gritty. I have never felt more frustrated playing a game than when I played this. There are some gameplay flaws that made most segments in my first playthrough much more difficult than need be, especially on the hardest difficulty. 

The lightsaber combat, well... just sucks. After the first level, you'll encounter bigger and tougher enemies pretty often. These enemies have more health, don't flinch at your melee attacks and can perform attacks which your lightsaber cannot interrupt, which isn't bad in and of itself. What is bad, however, is the nonexistent animation cancelling which, if you don't know, is when the game interrupts an attack animation in favour of a dodge animation when you press the dodge button, provided you're not too far into the attack animation. I know what some people are gonna say: ''DaRk SOuLs dOeSn't hV aNImAtIon caNceLiNg EitHeR bUT yOu doN't hEAr peOpLe COmpLaIn!!". I WANNA PLAY A HACK N SLASH GAME AS AN OVERPOWERED FORCE WIELDER AND HAVE FUN, NOT BE MISERABLE. Remember when I said that Force Lightning will be your go-to? This is why. Against the tougher enemies, you'll often have to keep your distance, use your Force lightning until your Force bar depletes then wait for it to replenish and then you do it again. And again, until that SINGLE TOUGH enemy is dead. Boss fights unfortunately also suffer from this same tedium, especially [spoiler] Palpatine. [/spoiler] If you're up against multiple tough enemies, you just rinse and repeat the steps until they're all dead because if you decide to hack n' slash and the tougher melee enemies attack you while you're mid combo, you're as good as dead. You'll get knocked down and you might even stay down, all because you couldn't dodge away mid attack. Which brings me to my next point- 

The enemies are relentless in this game. The first level isn't too difficult but then it picks up. You'll face off against Junk Titans(?) Rancors, AT-ST's, a plethora of Stormtroopers of different variants which include my personal favourite: Purge troopers. The enemy variety is great but fighting them isn't. Most of them are resistant to your Force Grab so you can't launch 'em halfway across the map. They can knock you down even though you thought you were outside of their attack range. Once you get knocked down the enemies JUST. KEEP. ATTACKING. Sometimes even resulting in a stun lock because they'll barrage you with the same attacks that knocked you down in the first place. This is not helped by the fact that it takes forever to get back up in the first place. You kinda just lay there for 1-2 seconds which is seriously enough to get you killed on the harder difficuties. 
[spoiler] I had to restart the last level about 6 times before I could progress because at the very beginning, you'll be met with FOUR WAVES OF ENEMIES, EACH OF WHICH CONSIST OF AN AT-ST AND ALL THE STORMTROOPER VARIANTS. I ran around the room jumping and dashing for 5 minutes just electricuting all the tough enemies until they were all dead and let out a sigh of relief just before I was shot in the back and met with another wave of them. Then another. And then another. [/spoiler] Purge Troopers are the worst. They can fire missiles that deal lots of damage, have incredible tracking and can knock you down. Oh, and they can fire at you from a pretty great distance. And if you die, and you will die, you'll respawn at a checkpoint - a checkpoint that is often placed right before an unskippable cutscene so you'll have to watch that cutscene again every time you die.

These were my main gripes with this game. And I think these components are what make a good Hack n' Slash game which this game failed to get right. Since it really didn't have much going for it, it really needed to polish the things that I think are integral to this genre. It has a sub-par story, level design, and character building. Starkiller is a definitely a cool character and Sam Witwer's performance is pretty alright. But that's about it. 

TL;DR: 
[i] Pros [/i]
a) Fun force powers
b) Great physics 
c) 3 Physics engines working in tandem make for a better gameplay experience
d) Cool main character and performance

[i] Cons [/i]
i) slow, unresponsive feeling melee combat i.e. no animation cancelling
ii) Enemies are dumb OP on harder difficulties and are relentless. Can stunlock you and kill you easily when you're vulnerable
iii) Checkpoints are placed before an unskippable cutscene
iv) Most fights are mired in tedium since you have to just spam your force lightning instead of playing with you cool lightsaber because of (i)
v) sub-par story and side characters
